subsubtopic: REQUEST SUBJECT OF RUNAWAY SATELLITES BE REFERRED TO UNITED NATIONS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House urges the Canadian government to refer the subject of runaway satellites to the United Nations Security Council in order to strengthen systems for early detection and public warnings about radiation hazards, so that public safety can be improved and proper apportionments made in the fiscal responsibility for clean-up operations which, in the present case of the Russian Cosmos satellite, have resulted in heavy and unfair expenses to Canada.

speechtext:

That this House urges the Minister of Veterans Affairs to introduce the necessary amendments to the Pension Act so that the compensation for prisoners of war provided therein will apply to the fewer than 200 Canadian veterans still living who were prisoners of war during World War I, as it does to those who were prisoners of war during World War II.

subsubtopic: REQUEST AGRICULTURAL JOBS BE IMPROVED-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43,1 seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that many farm workers are currently being victimized by the Department of National Revenue and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, that they are refused benefits by the officials of these government organizations on the grounds that their type of employment is not insurable, and that this state of affairs is particularly affecting our young people who will assume tomorrow the farming responsibilities in this country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House urge both the Minister of National Revenue and the minister in charge of the Unemployment Insurance Commission to take immediate action to eliminate the many obstacles which prevent the employment of farm workers from being insurable.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It is very simple. Will the Minister of Finance indicate what he anticipates to be the inflation level, average 1978 over average 1977? I ask this as a UPI story yesterday indicates that the minister has said it will be approximately 8 per cent.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the story is not correct. I said by year and we expect the inflation rate will be 6 per cent on average during the year. I explained that I could not make a precise prediction, but I can say it will be between 6 per cent and 7 per cent.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext:
On November 18 the Minister of Finance very definitively told the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs:
For the totality of the year 1978 it is going to be an average of 6 per cent.
That is a mark-up from his October 20 statement. Will the minister indicate why he is getting away from the 6 per cent ceiling target which he initially set on October 20, bearing in mind he has asked Canadian workers to accept a 6 per cent ceiling as far as their wage increases are concerned?

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is because in the CPI of the last few months imported fruit and vegetable prices were higher than we predicted.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: As of last night, excluding the passage within one day of Bill C-23, the employment tax credit bill, the minister had absolutely no legislation before this House with regard to anything that might relieve the unemployment situation or the inflation situation. Have we seen the total package of government measures as far as financial relief is concerned, and unemployment, and are Canadians who are suffering from inflation on their own as far as the government is concerned?

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday we discussed with the ministers of finance the short-term and medium-term policies for Canada.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: How about the immediate?

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INFLATION IN 1978
speechtext: Yes, we discussed the immediate. I was very pleased to see that the minister of finance for the province of Ontario, Mr. McKeough, was in complete agreement with our policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. Last October the minister was quite definite in his forecast of a 6 per cent rate of inflation for 1978. He revised that in the House today to somewhere approaching 8 per cent.
Six to seven is not eight.

I can further support my argument by telling the minister that inflation is now running at an annual rate of 9.5 per cent, according to the last CPI or, based on the last three months, at a quarterly rate of 11.5 per cent. Therefore, an 8 per cent rate of inflation is logical to accept. Is the government now going to change its economic forecast in order to preserve what little credibility it has left?

Mr. Speaker, we have made an economic statement on October 20 last and we have forecast that the economic growth would be in the vicinity of 5 per cent with an inflation rate of 6 per cent at the end of the year. We will not change our projections. My advisers, as well as most economic commentators, agree that 1978 will be better than 1977 and that only Japan could have a better economic performance than Canada.

As we approach the end of the government's ineffective anti-inflation policy there is a special need for Canadians to be able to place confidence in economic forecasting. Would the government consider asking Statistics Canada
January 27, 1978

to postpone its anticipated change in the base for calculating statistics from 1971 to 1974, so that there will be no statistical hanky-panky or shell game going on at the time an election is called.

Mr. Speaker, I am not in charge of Statistics Canada. I know it has always behaved as a very responsible agency and that it is not submitted to government directives in its professional activities. So, if it plans to change anything, I was not made aware of it. But I have confidence in Statistics Canada because it has always been honest with the Canadian public.

Would the minister recommend to his colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and to Statistics Canada that they devise a new method of measuring inflation, something akin to a poor persons' index, so we might have an opportunity during the post-control period to measure the full impact of inflation on the more than one million Canadians who are unemployed, on the working poor and on those living on fixed incomes?

Mr. Speaker, I have confidence in the professional integrity of Statistics Canada and I am surprised that the hon. member now asks the government to interfere with an agency which has such a good reputation.
Macmillan bloedel, b.c.-proposed shutdown of mill-government POSITION

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. With his well known concern for the plight of the unemployed, would he tell the House what his response was today to the announcement by MacMillan Bloedel, the largest forestry company in British Columbia, that it intends to shut down the Vancouver plywood mill, with a loss of 700 to 1,000 jobs on the lower mainland? What steps has he or the government taken to intercede with the company? Can he now report to the House whether the shutdown will, in fact, take place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Immediately I received the information from the corporation, officials of my department were on the site explaining the facilities which were available. The union and management have met with provincial government representatives, and the company has agreed to a stay of 30 days before a final decision is made. I believe something like six months' notice is required.
As I understand it, in the final analysis the company will be placing about 250 of the 700 workers affected in the White Pine mill and the mill at New Westminster. An additional shift will be put on to make this possible. The company
Oral Questions
believes that it can place within the corporation about another 150. If these numbers hold, given the six months time frame I think hon. members will see we can handle this problem very effectively.

Might I point out that this company has received from the government, in corporate tax concessions over the past eight years, in excess of $11 million. That money was provided for retooling and measures to make the company s operations efficient. The reason given by the company for the shutdown is that the mill is too old and cannot compete. In discussing this matter with company officials, has the minister brought to their attention the value of the grants, concessions and gifts they have received from the government without them being tied to jobs? Is it the minister's position that in future such grants, concessions and research money will be tied to the provision of continuous employment?

The hon. member knows as well as I do the conditions which have existed in that industry. He knows the softness of the market in the United States and the difficulties the industry has had to face. I think it is appropriate for a government to make such grants in order to keep the majority of the work force in a particular company employed.
The fact that they are able to move into a third shift at the White Pine and New Westminster plants is an indication that they are not shutting down but are, in fact, expanding. If that is one of the reasons given-and it has not been given to me personally-we will, of course, remind them of these particular grants and ask them to what extent they have made any effort to make that particular plant operational and to keep it up to grade.

Mr. Speaker, the minister did not answer the question as to whether government policy is that these research moneys and grants should be tied to continuing employment. I point out to the minister that since the last budget of this government this company alone has received an additional $1.5 million in special tax concessions because of the inventory provisions in the last budget. Next year it will receive $2 million for that specific item alone. Is it the minister's and the government's position that we should continue to give out this corporate welfare for which the workers at those plants are paying, without tying it to some guarantee that there will be continuing employment for the workers?

Mr. Speaker, if we were not making these arrangements with corporations, the workers at those particular plants would probably be laid off in larger number. We are endeavouring to maintain employment at as high a level as we can. Where there is overproduction, we have to use the facilities we have in the Department of Employment and Immigration to see that workers are placed in other jobs where they can use their talents and skills.

January 27, 1978
Oral Questions
Macmillan bloedel, b.c.-government action to avoid

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. With respect to the 30 days to which the minister referred a moment ago, has the minister heard directly from union leaders in the area, especially Mr. Jack Monroe, to the effect that it may be possible to conduct a study of the mill in question but that it could not possibly be done within 30 days, and that over several months such a study might give rise to suggestions for modification and rationalization of the plant, which would enable the bulk of the workers to continue their employment?
The union desperately needs more time before the closedown, in order to carry out this study. Does the minister know about this? Has he been in direct contact with the management of MacMillan Bloedel and asked them to seriously consider an extensive delay of the closedown so that such a study could be carried out?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to one part of the question, Mr. Jack Monroe has not contacted me personally, nor do I think he has been in touch with our department to make that particular representation. I do feel, however, that there is a particular role for the union to play and we do not wish to usurp the responsibility of union leaders. The 30-day delay time is a time limit within which MacMillan Bloedel and the government will try to determine if it is possible to keep this operation going. But the notice is six months. The lay-offs will not take place until that length of time has passed. That will give the company and the union an opportunity to see if, in fact, these on-site jobs can be saved, rather than transferring workers to other regions.

I thank the minister for that answer. Has the minister been in direct contact with the management of MacMillan Bloedel and, if not, would he be prepared to contact Jack Monroe of the IWA to discuss this matter with him and bring to the attention of MacMillan Bloedel the fact that the union believes there must be a further extension of time in order to resolve this problem?

Mr. Speaker, Mr. Monroe's talents and abilities as a union leader have received high commendation. I am sure he is aware of the situation and feels that as leader of this particular union he can take that message directly to the company. It is a matter of mutual interest. I do not think Mr. Monroe needs my intervention, but if he does in this case I would be happy to meet with him and with management if that would help maintain jobs.

subsubtopic: CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-SPEEDING UP IMPLEMENTATION OF PHASE THREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
As jobs are particularly hard to find at this time of the year, which makes life exceptionally difficult for the unemployed in search of work and who are denied insurance benefits because they do not seek employment-it is somehow like a mother sending her child to pick strawberries in the month of October: there is no way he will find any-can the minister tell the House whether phase three of the Canada Works program can be launched a few weeks earlier to allow the creation of a larger number of jobs and so give workers the possibility of really earning their living through work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-SPEEDING UP IMPLEMENTATION OF PHASE THREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have indicated that possibility to our staff when people are looking for a job. We have therefore
decided to do so; I got in touch with every hon. member advising him of our intentions with regard to phase three of the Canada Works Program.

subsubtopic: CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-SPEEDING UP IMPLEMENTATION OF PHASE THREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary.
As recently as this morning, it was reported on the air waves of a radio station that phase three of the Canada Works program would be delayed. I should like to ask the minister whether the program as announced, will be implemented and whether it will start at the time indicated by him. In addition, can the minister tell the House whether a decision has been made with regard to the amount of money to be spent on phase three and, if so, can he inform the House of it immediately?

subsubtopic: CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-SPEEDING UP IMPLEMENTATION OF PHASE THREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize, but I shall have to make my remarks in English because technical terms are involved.

We have decided that within the Canada Works program we will build an economic growth component of about 30 per cent to create more permanent and long-term jobs. This has come about as a result of representations from both sides of the House and from the business community. In addition to that, the President of the Treasury Board has announced the $150 million labour-intensive program, and just yesterday we passed the employment tax credit bill. There is approximately $700 million in place now for the direct job-creation aspect of the program, to say nothing of the approximately $ 1 billion for training programs which are in place. All these measures are directed toward assisting the unemployed in the hope of getting them back into the work force.

January 27, 1978

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission. As the minister has stated, we must do everything we can to deter and prevent fraud and cheating in respect of the UIC program. Is the minister relying entirely on his $ 1 million advertising compaign to stop abuses of the program, and does he believe advertising will stop criminals from embezzling UIC funds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think advertising will stop criminals from doing anything. What we are trying to prevent is the idea on the part of individuals that it is a lark to cheat their fellow workers, and who in fact become criminals or acquire criminal records. The Auditor General indicated that we have to tighten up on administration, and we are in fact doing that. Any study of the statistics will indicate just how effective we have been in that area. It seems to us-and this is in keeping with what the Canadian Law Reform Commission indicated-we have an obligation to advertise and get the message across to those who pay the premiums that certain benefits are derived from the unemployment insurance program, but there are also certain obligations. The fact that we are moving in a more effective way and in a better administrative fashion is a reason, I think, for putting people on notice that to steal is to be a criminal, and this is what we want to prevent. It is not a lark to steal from your fellow workers.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the advertising campaign would indicate the government has failed in its responsibility
Oral Questions
to see that no one cheats under the scheme. Will the minister consider appointing a special investigation division, perhaps better known as a fraud squad, which the minister's officials and federal security officials say is badly needed because the UIC is extremely vulnerable to individual and organized fraud?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a very careful examination of our record on the administrative side will indicate that the conclusions reached by the hon. member are incorrect. We have a most effective administrative authority in place, checking on this particular aspect. Because it is becoming effective, and because of the number of investigations under way and the number of prosecutions which have come about, it seemed appropriate to get the message across to people who are paying premiums so that they will not get caught in that particular net.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as security advisers to the Prime Minister and RCMP officials have stated that only a small portion of internal and external UIC fraud is being uncovered, do they believe advertising is now the answer?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING ON PREVENTING FRAUD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied they believe advertising is one of the answers. We had an overpayment of approximately $65 million. We were effective in getting back $60 million of that $65 million as a result of the enforcement and administrative procedures which we have in place. It is more important to prevent that kind of operation so that it does not cost the premium fund money to go after those who are cheating under the program. It is a very small percentage when one talks about $3 billion to $4 billion of payout and $65 million to $95 million of overpayment. We can save a lot of money if we can prevent cheating rather than having to collect afterwards.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration regarding the advertising program. Something less than .3 per cent of the Canadian people are being aimed at by this advertising campaign. Why would the government want to waste $1 million by advertising to all Canadians when it would be a much less costly scheme to put inserts with cheques or have endorsements on the back of cheques? After all, the only people who can cheat are those receiving benefits.
The old pork barrel is right there, Bud.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is obvious the opposition feels we are in an election year, because they are trotting out all the old phrases.
Hear, hear!

Does the minister know what he is doing?

January 27, 1978
Oral Questions
Very definitely. There were 6,200 cases last year, involving approximately $60 million, so we are not only talking about a small percentage.
Sixty million?
The small percentage might be applicable to this year. If we can prevent that kind of thing, it is a good investment for the premium account.
Mr. Speaker, is the minister willing to name the advertising agency which will collect the $200,000 fee for placing these advertisements?
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I cannot give the hon. member the information off the top of my head, but I will send him a letter. It is public information.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my answer is that this issue is under study. Concerning the precise points mentioned by the hon. member, I cannot guarantee that they would not be applicable in the future. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised the minister does not know, because program co-ordinators in some towns have already been given the regulations for 1978. subsubtopic: ONTARIO-DAMAGE CAUSED BY STORM-REQUEST FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. I am sure he is very much aware that Ontario has suffered extraordinary weather conditions this winter. Yesterday, much of Ontario suffered from the worst storm in 20 years, a storm which caused several deaths and millions of dollars of property damage, much of which will not be covered by insurance. The storm disrupted the lives of millions of Ontarians.
In view of the extraordinary circumstances caused by the storm, is the Prime Minister prepared to extend to the affected businesses, municipalities and individuals extraordinary financial assistance on behalf of the Government of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ONTARIO-DAMAGE CAUSED BY STORM-REQUEST FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a well establish policy of assistance to provinces in defined circumstances. When, through natural causes such as this, they incur great distress the government is always anxious to come to their assistance. The first rule is for the province affected to apply to the federal government for assistance, and we then study the problem. As the hon. member knows, in a large number of cases the federal government has assisted the provinces in circumstances such as those described by the hon. member.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO-DAMAGE CAUSED BY STORM-REQUEST FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. As the Prime Minister is probably aware, President Carter of the United States has designated some states as disaster areas. subsubtopic: ONTARIO-DAMAGE CAUSED BY STORM-REQUEST FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:

I would remind the hon. member that just a few years ago in northern Ontario - I believe, in the Sudbury area - a natural disaster occurred

which called for the assistance of the federal government, and we were very forthcoming.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
I was downstairs at another meeting, when I received notice that Your Honour was ready to proceed with my bill. I apologize if I have caused any difficulty to the House by being a few minutes late and causing this delay.
This is a very important bill. I believe there has been some discussion between the government House leader and the House leader opposite with regard to the debate today. I am delighted that it may be possible to move expeditiously on the bill during the course of the day.
I am pleased to introduce for second reading today Bill C-19 which amends the Petroleum Administration Act.
The principal purpose of this bill is to enable the government to fulfil its commitment to provide international prices for the synthetic oil produced by Syncrude Canada Limited from Athabasca oil sands. It enables similar treatment to be extended to the production of other selected domestic petroleum sources at the discretion of the governor in council, a very important provision. By introducing this legislation, the government is taking a further significant step to ensure that Canada's net dependence on foreign oil is reduced by encouraging the development of our petroleum resources.
Canadians are beginning to recognize the severity of the problems presented by the rapid decline of our conventional petroleum reserves. The National Energy Board report on Canadian oil supply and requirements of February, 1977, projects the expected fall-off in conventional oil supply, and the corresponding need for oil from other sources. It indicates that by the early 1980's the total supply requirements of Ontario and the western provinces can no longer be met by indigenous crude oil. By 1990, the board foresees Canadian oil providing only about 42 per cent of our oil requirements as compared with about 82 per cent in 1977.
This potential growing dependence on foreign oil will not only place a heavy burden on our economy by increasing our balance of payments deficit but also endangers our oil supply security by increasing our reliance on sources which may be reduced or cut off by disruption of overseas production, as happened in 1973, by an embargo, or simply because of world demand beginning to outrun available supply.
Energy
It is imperative that we limit our dependence on foreign oil. It is therefore a cornerstone of national energy strategy that we restrict our net dependence on foreign oil by 1985 to no more than one third of our domestic demand or 800,000 barrels a day, whichever is lower. This means we have to take advantage of a number of opportunities available to us. We have to lessen oil consumption through conservation measures. We have to find substitute energy resources to replace oil, particularly foreign oil. We have to find new supplies. In particular we must recognize the potential of our heavy oils and of our tar sands out west. The government has already taken action to reach some of these targets. I believe it should be possible to produce close to a million barrels a day from the tar sands and heavy oil sands out west by 1990. I believe Canadian industry is gearing up to meet such a target by that date. I think the date is a realistic one. There are some who suggest it may be somewhat optimistic. Well, I think the problem we are facing requires us to reach for a target of that kind. The government has already made a commitment.
Steps which have already been taken by the government include the following:
1.	A commitment to move Canadian oil prices toward international levels in order to encourage conservation and resource development.
2.	The establishment of a comprehensive program of energy conservation which is already showing results in terms of reduced energy demand.
3.	The creation of a financially attractive environment for oil and gas producers.
4.	The conclusion of a deficiency agreement with the Interprovincial Pipeline Company which allowed the company to raise the funds to extend its system to Montreal. This gives Montreal refineries a secure supply of domestic crude oil into the 1980s.
Other measures which the government has taken include the formation of Petro-Canada to stimulate activity in petroleum exploration and development and our support for the Syncrude project by way of equity participation and the assurance of international prices for its output. The principal purpose of the legislation I am introducing for the second reading today concerns this latter step.
Consequent upon the withdrawal, in December, 1974, of Atlantic Richfield Limited as a participant in Syncrude, negotiations among the remaining participants, the federal government and the governments of Alberta and Ontario, culminated with the signing of the "Winnipeg Agreement" on February 3, 1975. As a result of this agreement the federal government acquired a 15 per cent equity interest in Syncrude, and the governments of Alberta and Ontario 10 per cent and 5 per cent respectively. In addition, the federal government undertook to assure to all participants the availability of international crude oil prices on the sale of synthetic crude from the Syncrude project.

January 27, 1978
Energy
Production is scheduled to commence this April, with daily volumes rising to 108,000 barrels a day by June, 1980, and then to 129,000 barrels a day. That is the rate of capacity on the basis of existing engineering. There is also the possibility that this production could be further expanded to a level of
200,000	barrels a day. Participants are currently considering the marketing alternatives of disposing of their shares of Syncrude output. To allow sufficient time to complete marketing arrangements before the first product becomes available it is necessary to put in place the mechanism to be employed to afford international prices to Syncrude output.
A number of mechanisms were considered. After discussion with the other Syncrude participants, including the provinces of Alberta and Ontario, it was decided that the objective could be best accomplished by permitting Syncrude output to be sold in Canada at international prices and then compensating refiners and other users as if the crude were imported. The calculation of the rate will be in line with the current methodology with respect to import compensation.
This approach will allow the international market to establish the value of Syncrude output relative to other crude oils. It will be comparatively easy to administer as it makes use of the existing compensation mechanism. The bill also authorizes the funding of this program by a levy on all crude oil refined in Canada and oil products imported to this country. This financial burden, equating to a maximum of approximately half a cent per gallon, will be placed on the consumer of petroleum products, who I believe should be prepared to pay the price to secure such development, both with respect to Syncrude and other petroleum energy projects.
I believe the mechanism I have just outlined for providing international prices is attractive, not only because it is consistent with our self-reliance objective, but also because it can be employed to encourage the future development of other energy projects.
Earlier I mentioned the need for Canadians to recognize the severity of the problems presented by the decline in our conventional petroleum reserves. We are fortunate, however, in having the option to develop the great potential of our vast non-conventional and frontier hydrocarbon resources. The oil sand and heavy oil deposits of Alberta and Saskatchewan, combined with our gas reserves in conventional and frontier areas, together give Canada a potential petroleum resource base which satisfy our country's energy needs well into the future.
I am encouraged to see that the Canadian oil industry is proceeding rapidly to develop these as yet largely untapped resources. Imperial Oil has recently announced a 140,000 B/D heavy oil project at Cold Lake. There are proposals to construct a 100,000 B/D heavy oil upgrading plant at Lloydmin-ster. Shell is examining the possibility of a third oil sands plant with a 125,000 B/D capacity in the Fort McMurray area. And Great Canadian Oil Sands is considering an expansion of its existing facility.

As I have said, the total cost of these projects runs into billions of dollars. The development of these resources may now seem expensive, but they will, as the world's conventional crude oil reserves decline, be cheap at the price. Canadians must recognize this and be willing to pay the price to ensure not only that the problems of the present are solved but also that the promise of the future is fulfilled. Moreover, by creating thousands of jobs both in their construction and operational phases, these projects will help our economy to recover from the present recession.
The bill also authorizes two other minor changes to the Petroleum Administration Act. It provides for payments of special compensation to importers of petroleum in cases of undue financial hardship. This provision would be employed in situations where the regulations did not foresee special types of circumstances faced by importers.
The bill also changes the name of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board to the Petroleum Compensation Board, which more accurately reflects the current duties of the board. That is a technical change. The board was originally established under the Energy Supplies Emergency Act to prepare and implement plans to handle shortfalls of petroleum in times of emergency. This function of the board ceased on June 30, 1976. Its current and ongoing duties involve the administration of the oil import compensation program plus the administration of the program to provide international prices for the output of Syncrude Canada, which 1 have just outlined.
This legislation represents another important step toward implementation of established energy policies designed to assure Canadians of adequate and secure future supplies. As such, I commend it to the House for its prompt debate and passage.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the House that the minister's reports on our discussions with regard to this bill are accurate. We have no intention of delaying this bill. We support the basic principle behind the bill, but there are a few remarks I would like to make specifically about the bill as well as about the minister's remarks.
I think it is worth reminding the people of Canada that this is the third in a series of bills resulting from the attempts of the government to come to grips with the question of petroleum pricing in Canada. The first was the emergency energy supplies bill, the second was the Petroleum Administration Act, and now we have this amendment to the Petroleum Administration Act. I wait with bated breath for the fourth of these attempts to come to grips with a policy on petroleum pricing in Canada.
I am sure the House recalls the very unpleasant history of the evolution of these bills and of this problem which goes back to September 4, 1973, when, after publicly declaring he would never take such unilateral action, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) unilaterally put a price freeze on crude oil, causing friction to develop between the province of Alberta
January 27, 1978

and the Government of Canada. This action ultimately involved other provinces as well and lead to a period of serious and debilitating friction between the federal government and the provincial governments which hurt the nation as a whole and caused severe economic hardship for individuals. It was very disrupting to the industry and resulted in some net economic loss to Canada. It is difficult to come up with a realistic price tag, but it would certainly be in the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. That is the cost of an inopportune, politically motivated declaration by the Prime Minister during that minority parliament. I hope we will never have to go through that kind of exercise again because the economy and the Canadian fabric just could not tolerate it.
I would like to comment on some of the remarks of the minister about the so-called great things the government has been doing for Canada in terms of energy. At least that was the tone of the remarks of the minister, and I take exception to that. In his opening remarks the minister pointed out that, according to the National Energy Board, by 1990 Canadian domestic supplies will account for only 42 per cent of total Canadian consumption. If that projection turns out to be true, it will have devastating consequences for this nation.
The cost of importing the oil necessary to make up the 100 per cent we will need is enormous. It is a cost we cannot afford. It is in the order of $7 billion or $8 billion, based on today's prices. If we add that to the $12 billion trade deficit we suffer in terms of manufacturing, we encounter an incredible combined trade deficit of $20 billion. We think a 90-cent dollar is a depreciated dollar, but that is an extravagantly high priced dollar compared with the dollar we will have if we encounter trade deficits of that magnitude.
It is unacceptable and intolerable that the government should casually say that we are going to import more than half our oil by 1990. Instead, aggressive initiative should be taken by the government to ensure self-sufficiency and that we import zero per cent on a net basis. That is not an Utopian ideal; we are unique among western industrialized nations because we have the potential to do that. No other nation in the western industrialized world, with the possible exception of Great Britain because of petroleum in the North Sea, has the potential to be self-sufficient. Canada does, and that gives us a unique opportunity.
If this government were to dissipate that opportunity through inaction or inappropriate actions, that would cause great damage to future generations, and that should not be forgiven. We have that potential, and our party feels that self-sufficiency is an absolutely essential policy. It is a fundamental cornerstone of an energy policy for this country.
The minister articulated some steps he and his government are taking which are supposed to help ease our problem. The minister talked about trying to lower demand through conservation. There has been some progress, but not nearly enough. We feel that a reduction in demand to 2 per cent annual growth is possible. The minister talked about finding substitutes, but we have yet to see any concrete proposals in that
Energy
regard. It is a high ideal, but until we see what the government has in mind, it is hard to comment.
The minister talked about finding new supplies, particularly tar sands and heavy oils, and he expressed the expectation of the government that by 1990 one million of barrels of oil per day would be produced from tar sands and heavy oils. Where did that figure come from? What is the basis for that figure?
The government has no policy with regard to tar sands and heavy oils. The government has stated that it will treat each project in an ad hoc fashion. How can developers allocate resources when they do not know what the rules are? Companies are faced daily with decisions on how to allocate their financial and human resources, and if they are considering tar sands and heavy oils and find a situation where the rules are not defined, they cannot calculate their returns. The government suggests they put together a plan or come up with a program, and it will talk about it, but who in his right mind is going to spend the $5 million, $10 million or $20 million which is necessary to put together this type of plan, only to come here on the odd chance that, after discussions with the minister and his officials, everything will turn out all right? That approach shows such a dismal ignorance about the operation that it is disturbing.
The minister apparently does not even know how many companies are interested in developing these heavy oils. He mentioned Imperial and heavy oils, that Shell is looking at another tar sands plant, and Great Canadian Oil Sands is expanding its plant. For the minister's edification I should inform him that Husky Oil and Pacific Petroleums are two other companies actively looking at heavy oils.

Yes, Exxon may be a hardship case like that. Again, there is a temptation to make some of the friends of the government look good through the use of this clause.
The minister indicated in his comments that this bill is specifically designed to allow Syncrude to receive world prices for its production. In fact the bill does not talk about Syncrude specifically. The bill states that the governor in council can designate any production as those imported and, therefore, eligible for the import subsidy. Why go through this exercise? There is no other tar sand plant that is going to be completed for years in the future. We do not know of any heavy oil plants that are coming up. Why not look at those cases as they occur?
It strikes me as strange and inappropriate that we in the House of Commons are again being asked to give this open-ended authority to the government to deem any production it chooses as imports and, therefore, eligible for the subsidy. Is

the government going to deem all the production from Petro-Can's producing wells, if it ever finds any oil, as imports in order to make that bottom line look good? How is this discretionary power going to be used? We should build into this clause some check back to the House so that, as producing facilities are added to the list to be deemed as importers, the House or a committee of this place will have an opportunity to examine and consider it before the fact rather than after the fact.
The other thing I should like to bring to the attention of the House, giving it notice, is my intention in committee to introduce a firm amendment to provide a termination date for this whole program. The Petroleum Administration Act was designed to administer over that period of time during which Canadian crude oil prices were less than world prices and it was necessary to collect export taxes, to pay the subsidy on imports, and so on.
It is government policy, which we support, to get out of the business of controlling oil prices eventually and let the market place dictate. At that point there is no further need for the Petroleum Compensation Board. The government took some pride in stating it took an awful lot of work to disband the Halifax Harbour Relief Commission which had been in existence for 60 years. Members opposite suggest it is extremely difficult to disband something once it has been created within this government. For this reason, why do we not build into this bill right now a provision to allow this thing to die gracefully and with dignity when its usefulness is finished, rather than carrying it on, in a way to which we have become habituated, almost in perpetuity?
It is my intention at the committee stage, and I hope to be able to convince government members of the advisability of this provision, to introduce a clause which will provide for the demise of the Petroleum Administration Act on June 30, 1983, unless a positive resolution of the House is introduced to extend that life for another five-year period. This would allow all the flexibility in the world, while providing for the dignified death of this organization once its usefulness is finished.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the Syncrude chickens which were hatched in 1975 are coming home to roost. Having been outbluffed and outwitted by two of the major oil companies into a give-away of public funds, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) finds it necessary to come now and tell the people of Canada that there is a bill which has to be met, there is a price which has to be paid for the deal which was concluded in 1975.
On January 24, 1975, Mr. Geoffrey Stevens in his column in the Toronto Globe and Mail stated, "This is one of the highest stakes poker games in Canadian history".
On February 4, 1975, when the then minister of energy, mines and resources made an announcement, I said, "This is the greatest sellout of our natural resources in the history of Canada". Every day which has passed since has reinforced
January 27, 1978

those two opinions. It has been the "highest stakes poker game". There is no doubt who won the game. It has constituted the "greatest sellout of our natural resources in the history of Canada".
The time has come for the government to present the legislation by which we shall have to pay. This is not only for Syncrude, because the bill gives sweeping powers to cabinet by order in council to allow levies to be placed and taxes imposed on many forms of oil, as well as giving grants and concessions for different kinds of oil. Thus, we do not know from this legislation how big the bill is. We do know the government is asking parliament to give it the authority to pay the bill. We are being asked to sign a blank cheque. We do not know what the amount of that cheque is going to be.
We have to begin to recognize that when we talk about the oil sands of western Canada we are talking about one of the world's greatest reservoirs of oil. This legislation is asking us to pay for having it stolen from us.
In the 1973 booklet entitled "Energy Policy for Canada", reference is made to the geological survey of Canada which estimates that there are up to 700 billion barrels of oil in the tar sands of western Canada. If it could be extracted, that represents a larger accumulation of crude oil than there is in the Middle East. At the same time the estimates quoted are to the effect that 65 billion barrels of this oil can be recovered with the present known technology. It estimates that some 15 billion barrels can be recovered at a price of $5 a barrel wellhead, and 35 billion barrels at a price of $6 a barrel. The same report indicates that at a price of approximately $8 a barrel we have up to 40 billion barrels of crude oil which are economically recoverable from conventional reserves.
I ask the House to look at those figures. They were given in 1973, and this is only 1978. Approximately five years ago these were the optimistic statistics which were given to the people of Canada concerning the great unlimited reserves of oil that Canada has. Today the minister indicated that we are now a net importer of oil, that in the matter of a few years we will be able to meet less than half our oil requirements and that our bill for imported oil will be a staggering one.
Not only did the government paint this optimistic picture, the oil industry was equally euphoric about our oil supplies for the foreseeable future. The Imperial Oil Company's annual report for March, 1973, read as follows:
In the current debate, the export of Canada's energy resources is being questioned: in effect we are being urged to bank our petroleum resources. Canada is not in any way deficient in energy resources. Our present energy reserves, using present technology, are sufficient for our requirements for several hundred years...
That statement was made less than five years ago. This misleading information was fed to the public assiduously for many years, deliberately to persuade a supine government to allow United States oil companies to ship 60 per cent of our oil production to the United States, despite the fact that geologists and academic authorities, who were familiar with the field, had been telling Canadians and committees of this House that within a matter of ten or 15 years Canada would
Energy
have to import a very large proportion of its oil requirements. That day is already here, and we find that not only do we not have these large reservoirs of oil, which were allegedly available with the present technology, but we are now going to have to pay through the nose for companies to develop some of our oil sands.
In 1973 when the OPEC Nations acted in unison to force up oil prices, the oil industry in North America saw an opportunity to hold the public up to ransom, with the result that the wellhead price for oil has risen from approximately $3 per barrel to $12.75 per barrel, which is an increase of over 400 per cent. Certainly no one could attribute a 400 per cent increase in the price of a barrel of oil to inflation or to the cost of producing that barrel of oil.

That is right. As the hon. member says, the reverse is true. It is this horrendous increase in the price of oil which reflects itself in the cost of operating a car, a truck or a diesel engine. It reflects itself in the price of electric power and of home heating. It affects our whole economy, and particularly the farming and fishing industries are affected adversely.
The rapid rise in the price of oil from $3 a barrel to $12.75 has resulted in a situation where we paid in 1977 about $1.8 billion for imported oil, and it is estimated that by 1985 we will be paying $6 billion for imported oil. We are only beginning to realize what this will do to the cost of living for Canadians when we see what the future holds for us in terms of what we are going to pay for petroleum products. We will then realize how we have squandered the large accumulation of petroleum products which we had and which we gave away at fire sale prices. One then begins to realize that we have not had in Canada a national energy policy which was devised and designed to serve the interests of the Canadian people.
Let me just take a few moments to run over quickly the history of the oil sands development in this country. In October of 1962 Great Canadian Oil Sands, which is a subsidiary of Sun Oil of the U.S., was granted permission to build a small plant to extract oil from the tar sands. Later they enlarged the size and in 1974 the plant showed its first profit on oil, which they were selling for $6.50 a barrel. They have been making a profit ever since without any subsidy. They are a smaller plant without the modern technology which Syncrude has, and yet they have been able to do quite well on the domestic price. Yet we are being told that Syncrude cannot produce for the going price, which at present is $12.75, and needs a guarantee of the world price, no matter what the world price may be.
In February of 1972 the Syncrude consortium, which was made up of Imperial Oil, Atlantic Richfield, City Services Ltd., and Gulf Oil, secured approval from the Alberta government for the construction of a plant capable of producing
125,000	barrels a day. They estimated the cost to be $750

In September of 1973, syncrude and the Alberta government announced that it was going to cost $800 million to build this plant and that it would commence production in 1978, with the Alberta government agreeing to invest $500 million of the taxpayers' money to build a power plant, a pipeline and all the infrastructure. In December of 1974, Atlantic Richfield announced that it was withdrawing from the Syncrude consortium because the estimated cost of the project had risen to $1.6 billion from the original $750 million estimate.
On January 16, 1975, the remaining partners of the Syncrude consortium threatened to drop the whole project unless a partner could be found who would put up $1 billion to get the plan started on its way toward completion. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), and premier Lougheed of Alberta appealed to Syncrude for a 60 to 90 day extension to give the government time to canvass the situation to see what could be done. That reasonable request was refused, and so a hasty meeting was called in Winnipeg on February 3, 1975.
On February 4, the then minister of energy, mines and resources, the hon. member for Rosedale, announced that an agreement had been reached under which Syncrude would get the following concessions. First, they would get $600 million of equity, which was to be made up of $300 million put up by the federal government, $200 million by the government of Alberta, and $100 million from the government of Ontario, plus a $200 million loan from the government of Alberta which could later be converted, if it chose, into equity.
The second concession was a remarkable tax concession by which the company could go back to the terms of the 1973 budget, by which they received greater exemptions, were allowed to charge their royalties against their income tax payments, and were allowed lower rates of tax than were imposed in the 1974 budget. These tax concessions were worth to Syncrude, and are worth today, hundreds of millions of dollars which represent a loss to the Canadian treasury and which must be replaced by levying higher taxes on the other taxpayers of this country.
The third concession was that there would be no limit on the production of the Syncrude plant in the event that any pro rata plan were introduced by the government of Alberta, and the fourth concession was that Syncrude would be guaranteed the international price for any oil that it produced, irrespective of what the domestic price might be in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned for lunch I was in the process of pointing out that, as a result of the agreement which was reached on February 3, 1975, between the Syncrude consortium and the governments of Canada, Alberta and Ontario, it was decided to proceed with the construction of the Syncrude plant for the extraction of oil from the sands of western Canada on the basis of four concessions. I was enumerating those concessions when we recessed.
The concessions were that the three governments concerned would put up $600 million, plus another $200 million loan from Alberta; that Syncrude would get special tax concessions which would take them back to the 1973 budget; that they would be guaranteed no limits on their production; and finally, that they would be guaranteed the international price for the oil they produced. I think it should be noted that when we say they will be guaranteed the international price we are really asking this parliament to give the government a blank cheque and to guarantee to this company amounts of money that we have no way of computing.
When the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works was discussing this matter with the former minister of energy, mines and resources, I produced a copy of one of the studies done for the government of Alberta by Foster Associates. The minister of that day took no exception to the fact that the study based the economic feasibility of the Syncrude project on the assumption that the price they would get would start at $15.50 per barrel and would go up to reach $35.00 per barrel eventually in the last year or two of the life of the plant.
I think this House and the people of Canada should be given some idea of what we are underwriting when we say we are going to guarantee this company will receive the international price. That price now is above the domestic price. The minister said today, and has said before, that he wants to see this country get to the international price. We had better know what we are talking about; we are talking about prices far in excess of anything we have ever dreamed of in this country.
The strange thing is, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Canada entered into this Syncrude agreement despite the fact that it had never at any time commissioned an economic feasibility study, it had not hired any experts or called in any consulting firm to do an assessment of the project.
It is true that the province of Alberta had commissioned four studies, but none of those was available on February 3 at the meeting in Winnipeg. On the night before and on the morning they were meeting, a rapid summary was hurried to them by telex giving them a fragmentary picture of what the reports were going to say. The other two reports did not reach them until after the agreement had been entered into.
January 27, 1978

I think that the governments of that time were stampeded into entering into an agreement which was not in the public interest and for which we are now being called upon to pay. This legislation asks that parliament approve the power to impose a levy or tax on all domestic oil and on all imported oil in order to create a fund sufficient to pay the difference between the domestic price and the international price.
I notice the minister now uses the term international price. His predecessor kept using the phrase internationally oriented price. We used to try to get him to define it. It is not defined yet, and it is not defined here. One of my objections to this legislation is that almost everything is left to the discretion of the government, and its boards, and it has no real definition of what we mean by international price or on what it will be based. There is no indication at all of the types of oil to which it will be applied. As a matter of fact, if I understood the minister correctly, he said this morning that the cabinet would have power by order in council to apply it to any type of oil it wished. I assume the government can apply it to oil extracted from the heavy oil deposits in Cold Lake and Lloydminster. It can apply it to any particular company which has some problem.
There are very wide discretionary powers of taxation. There are arbitrary powers which I doubt any parliament should give to a government. But most serious of all it means that these powers will enable the government to give the same concessions to other companies which may develop the oil sands. As a matter of fact I do not see how it can refuse. The minister's predecessor kept saying that no commitment was being made with respect to other companies that might go into the tar sands to extract oil. Will it be possible to do that?
I notice from press reports that Shell Oil is now negotiating with the government of Alberta with a view to building a plant there. I hope it does. This country certainly needs the oil, and we certainly cannot afford to import the amount of oil we are importing now with the effect it is having on our balance of trade and on the Canadian dollar. But how will this government justify saying to Shell Oil, "We are not going to give you any international price; we are giving it to Imperial Oil, we are giving it to Gulf Oil because we made a mistake on February 3, 1975, when we were stampeded into reaching an agreement"? Will it say "We are not going to give it to you"? You cannot do that. There will be other companies, Husky Oil and others which may decide to build plants in the oil sands area and surely they will be able to claim in all justice that they should have the same concessions, and those concessions are going to cost the people of this country tremendous sums of money.
I think what should be recognized is the concessions which were made on February 3, 1975. First of all they consisted of these very large sums of money, some $800 million, $600 million in equity and $200 million in loans. These companies will have had and will continue to receive hundreds of millions of dollars out of the public treasury as a result of the tremendous tax concessions which have to be paid for by the other taxpayers of Canada. Now on top of that we are going to tax
Energy
the consumers of this country to give to Imperial Oil and Gulf Oil a special price for oil that is not enjoyed by other companies and is not enjoyed by the only other company that is producing oil in the tar sands, namely, Great Canadian Oil Sands, which has been producing all along, producing at the domestic price and with a much less sophisticated plant.
If ever a couple of oil companies have had preferred treatment, it is certainly Imperial Oil and Gulf Oil, under this agreement. I am saying to this House that these two companies and the oil industry as a whole just do not need this kind of handout. They have had the privilege given to them by this government of increasing the price of oil fourfold over the last five years. They have made hundreds of millions of dollars out of the Canadian people from their increased revenue.
Let me draw to the attention of the House for a moment the government's own monitoring survey for 1971-1976. I will have a chance to deal with it in more detail when we come to Bill C-12. To quote from page 5 of the monitoring survey, there is one sentence which I think ought to be emblazoned all across this country:
Over the 1971-1976 period internal cash generation for the monitoring aggregate totalled $13.3 billion. Of this total, $6.7 billion or 50.4 per cent is represented by after tax profits.
I ask the members of this House: do you know of any other commercial operation or any other industry in Canada where its profits represent over 50 per cent of its total cash revenue? Do you know of any store, any businessman who, out of his total cash take, receives over 50 per cent in after tax profits?
President Carter said a short time ago that the oil industry in the United States was robbing the American people. Well, he ought to have a look at this statement and see how it is happening in this country. The oil industry in this country has made so much money out of the profits it has had from its domestic production that I claim that Imperial Oil and Gulf Oil do not need this extra money which is going to be provided by levying a tax on the Canadian people. It depends on what the world and domestic prices are, but if the difference between the two prices is three or four dollars per year then the Canadian consumer will have to pay $140 million to $150 million a year more than he is paying now.
Mr. Speaker, everyone knows we have already put a tax of ten cents a gallon on gasoline and home heating oil in this country. We are already taxing our people very heavily. In addition, we are going to tax them because a consortium in Canada is extracting oil from the tar sands and has managed to get a commitment from the Government of Canada, not just that it will get hundreds of millions of dollars of money which the public treasuries have poured into that consortium, not just that it will get these tremendous tax concessions, but that it is going to get a guarantee of a world price, something no other company in Canada has. It is going to get that no matter what happens. It is going to be paid for by the consumers of Canada who are already paying too much for both their motor fuel and heating fuel in light of what it costs.

I say that this is an iniquitous piece of legislation. Any government which has introduced it has lost all sense of shame.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has put his finger on one of the real problems of this legislation. Toward the conclusion of his remarks, he suggested in so many words that what we are being asked to do is buy a pig in a poke.
In his introductory remarks, the minister dealt with the particular situation of Syncrude. It might well be that a clear examination of all of the facts, and some indication as to the probability of what will happen in the future, might persuade this House that in the interest of doing something about the energy situation in Canada a certain type of arrangement should receive the support of the House.
I consider it most improper, and I think I would not be discharging my responsibility to my constituents and to the people of this country, to accept, without something more being done to bring home to us the actual facts, the statement of the minister that we should relate the general to the particular and that this situation with regard to Syncrude justifies the passing of this legislation.
As a Conservative I thoroughly believe that the private sector in general is the best weapon, best means and best vehicle to sustain progress in our society. However, that does not mean 1 am automatically opposed to intervention by the state when it can be established to be essential.
I can cast my mind back a great many years to the inception of programs with regard to the development of the tar sands. Under the premiership of a very distinguished gentleman, later a law partner of mine, the late John Brownlee, the government of Alberta established a program with regard to dealing with the tar sands. The then expenditure in today's terms would appear an extremely modest amount of money each year.
A very considerable amount of the basic research and study was done with regard to the tar sands in the McMurray area. At that time the government of Alberta saw fit, in collaboration with one or two companies, to continue its basic research. This in due course led to what progress has since been made in the McMurray district.
This legislation is something entirely different. It applies to what I like to call the great skin game of 1973. Because of the

actions of the OPEC nations, the blindness, and possibly the collaboration of governments with some of the larger international companies, people on the North American continent and in Europe were frightened to death. They were persuaded to intervene in assistance, to engage in programs and to sponsor and enact legislation such as the Petroleum Administration Act and the energy allocation bill.
Several bills were passed at that time, having been introduced by the then minister, who has since left this House. At that time I participated very actively in the debate, both in committee and in the House. We attempted to move amendments. We said things then which have since been repeated by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). This shows that what the opposition stated at that time has now come true. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said, the chickens have come home to roost.
The legislation was conceived in panic, enacted in haste, and contained what at the time I characterized as an inordinate amount of authority given to the government. As a result of the power which the government took, against our opposition and contrary to the votes of the opposition, I never thought it would need to come back here. But now it comes back demanding an even greater degree of blanket authority on issues which may involve billions and billions of dollars.
The United States is in a very serious situation with regard to its balance of payments. President Carter has been attempting to secure enactment of a legislative package which will include, among other things, legislation dealing with the proposed pipeline coming down from Alaska, through the Yukon, into Canada. He has indicated that, if nothing is done, the United States may well have to contemplate a balance of payments deficit running into $100 billion or $125 billion in the not too distant future. I ask the House to consider what that might do to the question of inflation in the United States and, incidentally, to us, as well as the dangerous situation it would put those people in who directly rely on petroleum products for energy. We are heading down the same road.
I would like to feel that what the minister said might be correct, that a program such as he has intimated and such as has been referred to in the House might be essential in order to get this particular program going. However, we should be confronted with figures, particulars, an itemized statement, and some prognosis as to what will be involved. How will the people of the eastern provinces, who are faced with a staggering measure of inflation and unemployment, be involved, and how will they bear the burden of this particular program?
I know that if the production of petroleum were to cease the industrialized world would come to a crashing end because we have predicated our existence on the motor vehicle, on the internal combustion engine, and on the use of oil for fuel and heating.
I sometimes wonder whether in the excitement of these great projects which are pending we have not lost sight of their


ultimate cost and the effect this figure is likely to have on the balance sheets being presented. We have been talking about a gas pipeline coming down from Alaska through the Yukon into southern Canada. The cost has been estimated at between $13 billion and $14 billion. I notice that the other day in Washington some fairly responsible members of Congress suggested that between $20 billion and $25 billion would be more realistic. Of course that might be alarmist information given for political purposes, but I would suggest that whatever figure the minister presently has in mind he will have to double or triple by the time the pipeline is finished. What effect is the final figure likely to have on the inflationary spiral?
I,	for one, am not inclined to give the government the blank cheque it is seeking in legislation of the kind before us. I will make up my mind on the issue after hearing what the minister has to say during the committee stage. So far he has not been very informative. He is a good minister. He came into this Chamber just in time to inject a feeling of excitement about this bill and he read a very good brief which had been prepared by his officials-I do not know whether he had had a chance to read it before he delivered it. During the committee stage the missing information, part of which the minister may not have been able to soak up like a blotter, will be supplied by the officials who will be present to jog his elbow and put words and figures on his tongue-
