subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext: I have just had a holiday.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
The minister says he has just had a holiday. I have been on holiday too, in Yucatan, looking at the ruins, and now I have come back here to look at the ruins of the government. I might say that the ruins of Yucatan with their great stone faces were much more pleasant to gaze upon; at least they did not make the kind of speech the minister made today.
I once heard it said that genius could be defined as a capacity to take infinite pains. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should put that motto on his wall instead of the one which 1 imagine is there at the present time-"A Prime Minister can do no wrong". Ministers should be knowledgeable about the programs they bring before the House. They should know what they are doing, and why. There is more to this issue than the question of energy produced from oil derivatives under the present system.
Not long ago I was up in my constituency in the far north. I had a telephone call from a constituent, a farmer, who had conceived and developed a simple device for producing energy. He had a dozen cattle and he put the wastes from those cattle into a device which generated enough gas to provide electrical power for his furnace and for his lights. He has been in contact with both the provincial and the federal governments to work out a subsidy program through which the necessary equipment could be manufactured and sold to farmers at the price of $1,000 or so.
The beauty of this system is this: the end product is a valuable, highly enriched fertilizer which goes back into the field and is used to help grow feed for cattle. The cattle
Energy
produce wastes, and the cycle begins again, so there is a kind of perpetual motion. By this little story I am trying to show that there are a great many sources of energy still to be developed, for example, thermal power, wind power, solar energy. I know the minister has gone through his repertoire of what the government is doing in this field, but personally I am not convinced by his statements. I do not think he knows what the department is doing, and I doubt whether the department knows either.
The minister is right in saying petroleum products are finite. There are limits. Maybe there are 180 billion barrels in the east, maybe more-we do not yet know what advances may be made in measures of recovery. Within 25 miles of my own town on the Peace River the Shell Company-and I give the company full credit for this-has been working steadily on a pilot project to develop methods of utilizing the tar sands some
1,000	feet down. It is estimated that between 25 billion and 30 billion barrels of oil are secreted in the tar sands of the area. The great virtue of this experiment is that the environmental hazards associated with the operations at Cold Lake and elsewhere are largely avoided. Therefore we may look forward to a process of recovery of a much larger percentage of tar sands energy in Western Canada than either the minister or the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands contemplates at this time. We know, however, that the time will come when these reserves will be exhausted.
We owe it not only to our constituents but to those who come after us to ensure that adequate steps are taken and that money is spent under proper supervision to bring about a comprehensive program which will permit us not only to be independent but to be generously supportive of other peoples in the world who are in need of energy. We are one of the better equipped countries in the world, because of our experience, knowledge and expertise, to offer assistance. I include my friend, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, who is very knowledgeable in this regard. He is a scientist, and in his speech he gave sure indication of his knowledge.
I just do not like the ad hocery which this bill puts before us. The minister says this bill is to deal with Syncrude. It could deal with any situation. I will read some of the parts which are obnoxious and repugnant to me. Proposed section 65.13 says the following:
Where it is shown to the Governor in Council by the Board that it is in the public interest to do so-
Who decides what is in the public interest? Is it the board? This board has not shown the degree of knowledge and competence necessary to make an adjudication regarding public interest. It should be this House. It should be this parliament that should decide what is or is not in the public interest.
-the Governor in Council may ... exempt any petroleum or petroleum products from the charge imposed thereon ...
If this parliament has any task at all, surely it is to tax and to relieve from taxation, and not to leave it to any board to do so. For too many years we have dribbled away our powers to

Energy
the bureaucracy. The bureaucracy and the government are not composed of bad people. I think generally all governments are bad, but we should start on the basis that the men who conduct them are well intentioned but engage too much in deceit and are incompetent. I am not inclined to give this kind of power to people of that kind.
Surely it is the duty of this parliament to say to the minister that we will grant him this blanket legislation, but let him introduce into it a clause which says that any particular device, scheme or program with regard to any special area such as Syncrude shall be brought to the government by the board, and the government may indeed approve it by order in council, but subject to an affirmative resolution by this House. It is about time we started asserting not just our independence but also the necessity that we, as a parliament on behalf of the people of Canada, say to the government that programs of this kind which could involve over a ten-year period billions and billions of dollars will not be allowed to proceed without certain assurances.
We should not allow the minister to introduce them on his own, to deceive us, and to tell us about them only when they are all over. If the minister thinks he has a good program, let him bring it before parliament with facts, figures and detail, and if it is good we will give him our support. I believe that this parliament should reassert its independence from government. Hon. members opposite should assert their independence from the government and say that they have a right to be consulted about issues which affect us. I believe if that were done hon. members opposite could go back to their constituencies and be well received.
We are delinquent in our duty if we allow legislation of this kind to pass without making speeches such as the ones made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. There may not be profit in everything, but if we do not make those kinds of speeches, before ten years have passed I suggest that this House, this parliament and this country will be very sorry indeed for passing a bill of this kind.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill we have before us which deals with a special levy or tax on oil products in order that Syncrude may be compensated at world price levels for the oil production at its plant in the tar sands of Alberta is but one further instalment in a sad record of mismanagement of energy and tax policies on the part of this government.
In a sense this bill comes after the fact. In the original agreement with Syncrude the company was promised, no matter what, that it would get the world price for the oil produced from those tar sands. That price has not been guaranteed to any other Canadian energy producing company. Therefore this bill merely confirms something that was agreed to a number of years ago. We in the New Democratic Party objected to the Syncrude deal-or sellout, as we described it- and likewise we object to this bill for many of the same reasons.

I think it is worth while to refresh the memories of hon. members on some of the pertinent details relating to the agreement which lead to the bill before us. In late 1974 there was a crisis energy shortage in this country and in the United States, and there was great panic among consumers and government that we might see a repetition of the lineups of automobiles at gasoline stations and that people might freeze in the dark. In that panic atmosphere the government was forced into making a deal that in reality sold out the Canadian consumer and future generations in terms of assuring that our energy supplies would be controlled by the people of Canada, who own the oil or natural gas that lies beneath the surface.
In June of 1974 when oil companies only were involved in the planned project to extract synthetic oil-oil of a very high quality which costs less to refine than conventional oil-the cost of the Syncrude project was projected to be about $960 million. Then we found that by December of 1974 it had escalated mysteriously to $1.6 billion. Five weeks later, after one of the original partners in that private consortium of international oil companies operating in Canada pulled out, the cost jumped to $2 billion. By the time the government bailed out those multinational oil companies in the project the cost was well over $2 billion. That in itself should have led any astute minister of energy to question.
What happened was that not only had the oil companies manoeuvred this government; they had done so at a tremendously inflated cost. In the negotiations at that time the government was given an ultimatum; "Either pour money into this enormously costly project, or it will collapse and Canadians will be facing more serious shortages of energy, and there will be panic in the streets."
Along with the governments of Alberta and Ontario the federal government bailed out the Syncrude project by putting up tremendous sums of public money. This money was paid to the private companies. This party has argued in the past that energy is owned by the people and therefore should be controlled by the people. That principle has been accepted in every province with regard to electricity. The wisdom of having electricity owned by the public is no longer debated. Yet we still allow one of our most precious and important energy resources, oil, to remain in the hands of private companies.
The oil industry in Canada in terms of refining is 99 per cent foreign-owned, so not only is it in private hands, it is in private foreign hands. As a result we have the very odd situation of the governments of Canada, Ontario and Alberta pouring money in to help out these private companies. If I were a negotiator or sound businessman putting hundreds of millions of dollars into a project, I would want to get something from it in return, either in terms of ownership and control, or benefits in terms of the products produced. One would assume that the Liberal government would operate on that logical premise. But we know from the past record of this government in energy policy that logic does not prevail. In this
January 27, 1978

case it was a panic policy in a situation that helped the multinational oil companies.
Let us examine what happened. This project, involving more than $2 billion, was bailed out to the tune of some $600 million in investment money from the three governments; another $200 million in loans from the government of Alberta; another $600 million in assistance for the power plant and the pipeline from the public treasuries; and another $230 million in assistance for the building of roads and town services.
In addition to that kind of financial assistance in direct aid, the governments at both levels through their tax dollars gave the Syncrude partners tax concessions of immense dollar value; more tax concessions than private companies elsewhere in Canada were able to achieve. These included the writing off of provincial royalties, which has been denied every other company in computing taxes owed the federal government, depreciation allowances, and so on.
In return for all that capital investment and tax concession, how much ownership did we as the people of Canada obtain? I suggest it is not 50 per cent, not 60 per cent or 80 per cent, but a mere 30 per cent. We end up with 30 per cent control of the Syncrude project after putting up that kind of money.
When you total the grants and concessions and take into account the $1.4 billion of the more than $2 billion the private companies were supposed to have put in, you will find that we, as the taxpayers, are subsidizing even that amount. In reality we as taxpayers are putting up the majority of the money for the project but end up with only 30 per cent of the control. What a sellout! I do not see how the government can justify that kind of investment for that kind of control. It ends up with six directors on a board of 20, and 30 per cent ownership of a project in return for hundreds of millions in investment. The government was taken to the cleaners, and we as Canadians have, indeed, been taken to the cleaners along with it because we end up paying, in terms of our taxes, huge subsidies to Syncrude and, even more important, in terms of our consumer dollar we are subsidizing the Syncrude project.
What this means is that any refined oil product coming from Syncrude will now be subsidized to the extent of what the world price of oil will be. We are paying twice over for this project called Syncrude. Today the price of oil per barrel in Canada is $12.75. It is hard to believe that back in 1973 we were paying $3 a barrel for that oil. The world price which has been guaranteed to Syncrude is about $15 or $16, and the projections are that it will continue to increase. Therefore, because we have been able to cushion the world price for the Canadian consumer, holding it to $12.75, and the government will eventually bring it up to the world price now being received by every other oil company, we will allow Syncrude to get the world price. That is what this government has before us in this bill.
We as taxpayers have to make up the difference between $12.75 per barrel and the world price of $15 to $16. We are faced with an increase imposed in respect of other energy products we consume in order to pay Syncrude the equivalent of the world price.
Energy
We have already seen what has happened as a result of this tremendous escalation in the price of energy in the form of oil, from $3 a barrel five years ago to $12.75 at this time. It has been reflected in the cost of heating our homes, in the cost of public and private transportation, in the cost to the farmer for his machinery, which in turn is reflected in the higher cost of food, and in terms of unemployment. High energy costs have driven some of our industries into a non-competitive position. This has meant less sales and the layoff of many people.
We are paying many times over for this horrendous deal negotiated by the Liberal government. In return we are getting 30 per cent ownership and have to pay the world price for the oil produced by the Syncrude project. If ever there was an argument for full public ownership and control of the energy industries in this country, the Syncrude project is that argument.
We as the people of this country own the resources, but the policies of the Liberal and Conservative governments have been to pay the multinational oil companies large subsidies with our tax dollars and allow them to charge us the high world price for our domestic oil. What a ludicrous and ridiculous situation we have to face! It seems to me that the logic of seeing our oil industry as a public utility, as we do in respect of our electric industry, is very evident.
We now have this bill which will levy a tax or charge on conventional oil produced elsewhere in Canada in order to guarantee Syncrude the world price. What is that going to cost us as consumers? The bill does not spell this out, and that is another of the reasons we object to it. It gives carte blanche to the government to calculate what that charge will be. Several estimates report it to be $140 million a year in extra cost to Canadian consumers in the form of subsidies to the Syncrude project until we reach the world price for oil right across Canada. This is taking place at a time when inflation is on the rise and with unemployment at record high levels. To me this is a disastrous policy into which this government has locked itself.
We as consumers and workers have to put up with this immense folly perpetrated on the Canadian people by mismanagement. In addition, this means that we are going to be paying more for imported oil as the cost continually rises at the world level, and as we continue to import foreign oil instead of moving toward self-sufficiency, as we should have years ago. This is the result of the government allowing the control of pipe-lines to be in the hands of private industry. We have never moved toward an east-west pipeline in this country to isolate ourselves from the necessity of having to import oil from Venezuela and the Middle East. We will end up paying at least $1.8 billion a year for imported oil, as we do now, with the prospect of it going up to $6 billion by 1985. Already we have seen what this deficit in the balance of payments has done to the Canadian dollar. It has reduced its value to 90 cents. That will worsen, and indeed the consequences for our economy are very grim when one looks ahead. This legislation provides Syncrude with the world price, and one must worry about the projected world price a few years down the road.

January 27, 1978
Energy
Along with some of my colleagues in this House, I had the privilege of visiting the United States, specifically Washington and a number of other communities. We met with American officials to discuss its energy conservation program. In one of our meetings at the energy department in Washington with some of Mr. Schlesinger's officials, charts were pulled out which projected the world price, as well as what Americans were expecting to pay in 1985 for an imported barrel of crude oil. The figures were very sobering and were corroborated by other independent forecasters. It showed that by 1985 the world price, which is currently $15 a barrel, will be $25 a barrel in 1977 dollars and approximately $40 a barrel in 1985 dollars. This piece of legislation guarantees Syncrude the world price which has been projected for the years to come. Although Canadian oil will not cost that much to produce, we will end up paying Syncrude the world price because of this iniquitous legislation. The minister should resign in shame for this kind of betrayal.
The minister places great hope on the tar or oil sands as a great supplier of energy for Canada in the future. If one looks at the projected costs of such a development, one shudders because they amount to billions of dollars. I do not think the minister has looked at the oil sands situation from an energy point of view. The tendency is always to look at it from the dollar cost point of view. Has the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources conducted a study of the energy cost of extracting energy from the Alberta tar sands? Do we end up putting more energy into the tar sands in order to get energy back out and delivered to the consumer?
There was a study conducted by an American university on the whole question of the energy costs of the different developments which are occurring in the energy field. The oil shale situation was looked at by this group. I suppose that is not comparable to the oil sands, but it is an illustrative example and I hope the minister will provide a similar study at committee stage. The study group concluded that to obtain 1,000 BTUs of energy from oil shale, at least 1,238 BTUs of oil shale in the ground is required in the first place; another 359 BTUs of energy is required to build and to operate the extraction system, the great drag lines, etc.; and then another 483 BTUs of oil shale in the ground is required to supply the aforementioned BTU energy to build the system. In other words, an equivalent of 2,080 BTUs of oil shale is required to produce
1,000	BTUs for delivery to the consumer.
If that is placed on the energy equation scale, then is it worth while to invest so much money and time in that kind of extraction system or should we not spend our time and dollars on alternative energy sources such as solar, wind or enhancement of conservation? The government's record in that regard has been dismal, but in terms of alternative development we are behind most other countries in the world. From an energy point of view, as well as from a dollar point of view, perhaps we should go slowly into the future of oil sands development and look at alternative conventional sources of energy.

I reiterate our profound objections to the Syncrude project as well as the bill before us. It will continue to penalize Canadian consumers for the bad deal which was negotiated a few years ago. Indeed it gives the government and its anonymous officials a blank cheque and immense power in terms of defining the dollar levy consumers will end up paying to subsidize Syncrude. It gives wide and arbitrary power to cabinet. This cannot be allowed because the government has usurped the powers of this elected House. This will set a precedent for future oil sands development in terms of special deals, concessions, and prices for other oil companies involved in tar sands extraction, which no other energy company has in Canada. In its entirety this is a bad bill. The taxpayers will end up paying two times over for this very, very bad Syncrude deal foisted on the Canadian public a few years ago. I ask my colleagues to vote against it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) advocating public ownership. I do not think we can say that public ownership has always been within the public good, or that it has always been the most profitable in terms of goods produced and services provided. I do not think we can say public ownership is all bad. Each case has to be examined on its merits.
The Syncrude project is a rather unique partnership between two provincial governments, the governments of Alberta and Ontario; the federal government, which came in at a later stage in order to fill a vacuum that had developed; and the private sector. In terms of the future of Canada, it is a project of some considerable value. It does not lie in the mouth of any member of this House to condemn it, because its work is important in terms of the development of Canadian energy resources.
I do not intend to give the government an inordinately large pat on the back for its incentives in energy. I would be surprised if the minister did not come before the House indicating that he and his department are the next best thing since sliced bread. Some people have said that rather than sliced bread I should have used the phrase "sliced baloney", but ministers do this kind of thing.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie is right, however, that in terms of developing alternate sources of energy this government's record of talking on this subject in the House of Commons has been better than of taking any action. As time goes on our country will have to pay very dearly for the fact that thus far the development of alternate sources of energy has not proceeded too well.
What surprises me somewhat is the silence from the Liberal backbenchers on this bill which gives the government such extraordinary powers. I wonder how the Liberal backbenchers, who, I assume, are as concerned about the propriety of legislation as are any other members of the House, can sit by and allow a government to bring before the House a bill which may quite properly apply to the Syncrude project because of its
January 27, 1978

particular nature, but which contains provisions allowing the government access to the public taxing power with respect to private organizations and, indeed, access to public funds.
The bill is broadly based and, I think, is the product of a lazy draftsman. It is much easier to draft bills which apply to everybody, bills which grant powers which the government might not need in particular circumstances but which would give the government a lot of regulatory power, than to design legislation for particular cases. It should go against the grain of any member of parliament to accept a bill which, by its very terms, denies us the right to examine the use of public money and the use of public levying power. We are very concerned about that.
The provisions set forth in Bill C-19 may be perfectly all right for Syncrude because of the nature of that company, but this might not apply to other cases, and I think parliament should be at least in a position to be consulted about it. At present that is not the case with respect to this bill. In effect, the government is being given a blank cheque with respect to those other oil companies. That could be an advantage to the oil companies but it can also be a great disadvantage to parliament and to the taxpayers. If we have any job here as members of parliament, it is to watch that kind of matter very closely.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said that the job of parliament is basically a watchdog job; that the government creates legislation and comes to parliament to take part in the enactment of it, but that the first and foremost job of parliament is that of a watchdog. I am greatly surprised that some of the watchdogs on the other side are not equally concerned.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE IMPOSITION OF LEVY ON DOMESTIC PETROLEUM AND IMPORTS
speechtext:
That may be so but I am surprised that it is the case.
My predecessor in the role of House leader of the opposition asked the minister in an aside this afternoon whether he was in an amending mood. The minister said, quite properly of course, that he could not amend the bill on second reading. He is quite right that he cannot do that, but the question was not put to the minister lightly, nor was it with respect to amendments on second reading. The hon. member put his question with respect to amending the bill in committee.
I think it is proper that I lay out the matters that concern us with respect to this bill. We are very concerned about the clause with the notation in the margin "deemed importation" whereby, for the purposes of administering this statute, the product of the work of certain companies, the output from certain private organizations, can, by the stroke of a pen, be deemed to be importation and have the advantages set forth in the bill. We intend to address ourselves to that provision in committee.
The other aspect which concerns us regards the special subsidy for hardship cases. We are not suggesting that there
Energy
will not be hardship cases, but we are concerned about giving the government a blank cheque in that regard. Frankly, we do not want this kind of power in the hands of the government forever. When there is a difficulty which must be faced by any industry in Canada, the statutes should not be so broad as to allow the government to step in at any time and expend public funds without first coming to parliament. That is why we are here. If we do not believe we have the right to review this kind of expenditure-and this could be a massive expenditure- then I assume we should not be here. We intend to bring forth amendments at the committee stage so that this power, which the government clutches to its breast in this piece of legislation, is not granted to it forever.
We are also concerned about the length of time that this measure will be in existence. The life of this legislation can go on forever and ever until the government decides it is time to come to parliament and repeal it. In the whole period of time that I have been here the only bill I have heard repealed in the House is one dealing with the Halifax disaster. Governments do not repeal bills because they do not wish to denude themselves of power. We hope to advance during the committee stage an amendment in the form of the bill which will permit the House to determine, by way of an affirmative resolution, whether within a reasonable period of time this bill and its powers should continue in existence.
The answer to that might be that we will be taking up all our time debating these affirmative resolutions in the House. I want to say to the minister that it is not our intention to do that. If the government were to agree to this limitation in time, I would be prepared to advance the proposition that the affirmative resolution be dealt with without debate, and that would end the matter there. It is a very simple matter, and on the terms and conditions I have mentioned I think ought not to offend the government if it cares about the operation of this parliament.
I rise only to lay out in this general way, the conditions that will apply. We do not regard the matter of second reading as of too great importance in this case. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I decided to participate after listening to the response of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) to the speech of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes). It seems to me that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton needs a lesson in the rudimentary principles of private enterprise and capitalism. For the moment he will have to take that lesson from a socialist.
It has always been my understanding of sound business principles and of private enterprise and capitalism that whoever puts up all the money owns all of the project, and whoever puts up the majority of the money owns the majority of the project. I could hardly believe my ears when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton said that it was all right for this project we are dealing with to remain what he called a partnership; the public partners put up most of the money and the private partners have the majority ownership. I am sure his business friends would be horrified if he asked them to participate in that kind of deal. Perhaps I should find some investors and set up a plant to manufacture bologna slices and ask the hon. member to put up 70 per cent of the money and take only 30 percent of the ownership. I wonder if he would agree to that.
The Conservative party should be reminded that the Syncrude project is just another CPR; we are going to pay for it twice and still not own it. I read the debates of the 1880s in Hansard when the then Conservative government proposed putting up most of the money for the CPR. The Liberal opposition wanted to know why, if the government put up most of the money, they did not own it. When their leader was reminded that this would amount to public ownership he was horrified and, of course, when the Liberals took office they kept the deal going. The same thing is happening now. Twenty or thirty years from now our children and grandchildren will say the same things about Syncrude as have been said for almost 100 years about the CPR.
The government should blush when putting a proposition like this before us. And if the official opposition would only stick to the principles that I know they have, the bill would read differently. It would be bad enough if the government agreed to a limit on the world price to be received by Syncrude. Even if it were today's world price and nothing more, the company would still be laughing all the way to the bank and would end up owning the plant that we are paying for. That would be difficult enough to swallow but what they are offered is the world price on into the 1980s and 1990s. Mr. Speaker, how many times are the taxpayers to pay for a project they do not own? They do not even have a majority interest although they put up the majority of the money.

Many Liberal backbenchers have argued with me on occasion on the subject of sound business practices. I would be delighted to hear them object to this unsound business practice of a majority of public money going into an operation in which the public will have minority ownership. No self-respecting businessman would have anything to do with such a proposition.
How can a private enterprise government and a private enterprise official opposition who advocate sound business practices accept and perpetuate the nonsense offered in this bill? When I tell the Regina Chamber of Commerce about this they will be horrified. I do not understand how my colleagues in the official opposition and the Liberal backbenchers can hold still for this.
This is an economic tragedy, Mr. Speaker, and it will perpetrate social tragedy. It is a tragic example of "sell-out." It is a betrayal of new nationhood and sovereignty. I am a strong nationalist-not the old nineteenth century kind of nationalist-but by the gods of war, if we cannot control and run the development of our natural resources, particularly energy, I say we show weakness and cowardice. The government allowed itself to be held up to economic blackmail because of the threatened withdrawal or cancellation of the Syncrude project. There was a panic meeting in a motel room in Winnipeg when they gave away the store. What kind of Canadian nationalism is that? That is betrayal and leaves me ashamed and insulted. It is embarrassing for all of us but the minister and his colleagues. It would be nice to be a little mouse in the boardrooms of Imperial Oil, Gulf Oil and City Services and to be present during their cocktail hour to see them chuckle and rub their hands in glee at this marvellous return on investment they are receiving at the expense of the Canadian public as well as the concessions that they will receive through taxes and other benefits for years to come.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a real private enterprise deal for them, but it is not for us, and it is not for Canada. However, this government did not have the guts or the backbone to stand up and tell a few corporations; "Look, you either do the job or get the hell out of the way and we will do it ourselves." We can still tell them that, so that not only the government but the rest of us will be able to hold up our heads as Canadians with some measure of pride and say that we are developing and running our own resources for Canada first.
This kind of national betrayal which has occurred throughout the history of our country commenced with the CPR and now they are foisting on us another CPR. When I look at the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) I am reminded of the photograph of R. B. Bennett that Bob Edwards carried in the Calgary Eye Opener. Underneath the heading was "Another CPR Wreck". That is what we have in this legislation with the Syncrude project. I say to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and also to my hon. friend for Grenville-Carleton that you cannot stand up, support private
January 27, 1978

enterprise, sound business practice and principles, and then support an operation whereby we, the public, put up the majority of the money and have a minority of the ownership and a minority of the say, if any say at all. Surely we should have some backbone to put a stop to those kinds of supine and weak-kneed activities by a government which should know better, and does know better. It should be made to act better. This is an opportunity for all of us to do something constructive on behalf of our fellow Canadians, rather than ignore the weakness of some cabinet ministers who are carrying out an effort that will cause all of us to rue the day and pay the bill many times over.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR COLLECTION OF CERTAIN STATISTICS RELATING TO PETROLEUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
that Bill C-12, to require the reporting of certain financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of certain petroleum companies carrying on business in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased this afternoon to introduce for second reading a second bill, being a companion bill to the bill that has just finished its second reading debate and which will be voted upon next week.
Bill C-12, the petroleum corporations monitoring bill, concerns the vital matter of energy self-reliance. As I have indicated, it too is concerned with the increasing of Canadian supplies of hydrocarbon energy. As the title suggests, the purpose of the bill is the monitoring of the expenditures made by petroleum companies to search for and develop new energy supplies, which is a vital factor in our policy of achieving self-reliance.
From time to time members opposite, members from my side and the public generally are asking whether the oil companies are reinvesting their revenues so as to increase our own supplies of hydrocarbons and related energies in this country. If so, to what extent and how? The aim of this bill is to obtain the relevant data necessary to assure Canadian consumers, who must pay increasingly higher prices for petroleum products, that an appropriate proportion of the increased cash flow accruing to the Canadian petroleum industry is being reinvested in domestic energy related projects. This bill provides for a standard method of reporting of relevant capital expenditures and cash flow items by all petroleum companies in Canada which have gross revenues exceeding $10 million or total assets in Canada exceeding $5 million. It provides specific penalties for non-compliance or falsification of data.
Over the past three years there has been a great deal of discussion and debate about the energy crisis following the first round of crude price increases initiated by OPEC. In the winter of 1973-1974, for some countries, because of the embargo imposed by OPEC, the energy crisis was more than a crisis of price, it was a crisis of supply. It has been well documented that those countries, finding themselves in a position of near absolute dependence on this international cartel for petroleum supply, found themselves most vulnerable.
That supply crisis was underscored this past winter in the northeastern parts of the United States. Because of severe weather conditions and possible misjudgment by certain gas utilities, many cities in that region found it necessary to close schools and shut down industries in order that sufficient fuel could be allocated for the heating of private homes and hospitals particularly. The cost of this shortage in economic terms was enormous and served as a warning to both Americans and Canadians that any significant interruption in energy

January 27, 1978
Petroleum Statistics
supply is potentially catastrophic. Many Canadians were made all too aware of that catastrophic event because they were thrown out of work. Many of the parts manufacturers in the United States for the automobile industry are located in Ohio. Those plants had to shut down for the reasons I have mentioned. Energy supplies were feeding Canadian manufacturing plants and assembly plants just as they were feeding American plants; therefore, Canadians suffered also. The energy crisis was brought home, albeit in a very discriminatory way, to Canadians as well.
The question of more secure supplies in the future and the need to reduce our independence on foreign imports, as I said earlier this afternoon, which is related to moving our prices up both for reasons of conservation and new supply, needs to be examined against those cash flows which are being generated by the higher prices. This nation too is dangerously vulnerable to any interruption of energy supply, particularly of oil supply, in the future.
Major steps have been taken in order to achieve this goal of self-reliance. There was discussion this morning that self-reliance was not a particular objective which the lead-off Tory spokesman would like. I remind him that self-reliance is a much larger concept than the narrow one he has chosen. He has chosen to pin his faith on a very narrow concept.
The hon. member talked about self-sufficiency. It sounds great. However, when you look closely you see it implies all sorts of things such as supplies at any cost regardless of where they come from. I suggest to him that self-reliance is far more sensible and a far more effective objective of Canadian energy policy because it has a flexibility built into it. It recognizes that if we can get supplies from other sources and get them at a lower price than we can develop them in Canada, then we should take advantage of that option. His particular articulation of self-sufficiency would clearly rule that out.
If you push the hon. member's theme on self-sufficiency to its logical conclusions, you could not take advantage of cheap electrical power from the United States during the winter season. It would deprive a large proportion of Canadians of the advantage of cheap electrical power during the winter season in the same way that it would deprive the American consumer of power from Canada during the summer season when they have their peak load. 1 suggest the hon. member re-examine this from the narrow view that he has with regard to the objectives of the energy policy in this country.
To return to the goal of energy self-reliance, it is to allow for domestic petroleum and natural gas prices. One aspect of our policy to achieve the goal of self-reliance is to gradually rise toward international levels, to promote conservation, and also to provide the necessary financial resources required to develop an adequate supply base. That clearly is based upon the present fiscal system which is aimed at making a large flow of internally generated funds available to oil companies so that they can be invested in the search for and development of domestic energy sources.

In order to assure the accurate and useful measurements needed to assess the performance of this policy in stimulating increased exploration, a carefully designed cash flow monitoring program as stipulated in this bill is essential. The bill provides for a standard method of reporting for those petroleum companies to be surveyed on a semi-annual basis. A monitoring questionnaire, which reconciles our need for detailed information with our desire to minimize the administrative burden on the respondents, has been designed by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in consultation with industry members. Much of the information required in this questionnaire is available from no other source.
While the information obtained will, as a rule, be treated strictly confidentially, it will be the prerogative of the minister to disclose any or all of the individual company data in the House of Commons or elsewhere if, in his opinion, such disclosure is in the national interest. The moral value of the minister's powers to expose companies which do not use their financial resources provided by the Canadian consumer in the search for new energy must not be overlooked. An exception will be made where such disclosure will, in the opinion of the minister, impair the competitive position of a company. The minister will give every opportunity for a company to make representations as to the effect any disclosure might have on its competitive position before the final decision on this subject is made by him.
Certain penalties for non-compliance are prescribed within the bill and there is provision for selected spot audits of company records to be made at the discretion of those administering the bill. Officials conducting the monitoring survey will not disclose individual company data to any person other than the minister. The bill is an integral part of what we believe will prove to be a far-sighted energy policy that results in maximum net benefit not only to present but future generations of Canadians.
The cash flows accruing to the industry as a result of the increasing prices will doubtless continue to come under attack by many energy critics. It is understandable that, as allowed semi-annual price increases become reflected in pump prices, the Canadian consumer will perhaps become more concerned that the additional sacrifice he is asked to make should be a positive contribution in securing energy supplies for our economy, and rightly so. We believe that the readjustment entailed by the rising prices is inevitable for our society, and while it is important to minimize the disruptive effect of large price increases, through a gradual phasing-in program, the problem of future shortages in domestic energy supplies should be faced now.
The United States of America recognizes the potential havoc which any interruption of crude imports would have and is presently developing strategic petroleum storage reservoirs which will be filled largely with imported oil.
The strategic reserves of Canada can be developed at home. I refer in large measure to the tar sands and the heavy oils. The vast deposits of crude oil locked up in the tar sands, the heavy oil deposits of our western provinces and the untapped
January 27, 1978

potential resources of our frontier areas can supply this nation with the security of supply which Canadians in future years will require. However, that is going to require very substantial investment.
We believe that investment should be made by the private sector. We also believe that while the private sector has shown every inclination to re-invest those funds, it is essential in the public interest that parliament and the Canadian people have the legislative right to examine how those cash flows are being spent and whether they are being spent to the advantage of Canadians. It is the purpose of this bill to ensure that such surveillance can be carried out to the satisfaction of the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I shall naturally begin my remarks by straightening out the minister, if I can, as to the importance of terminology and as to the importance of understanding why self-sufficiency is an important policy objective. Based on the figures he gave this morning, by the year 1990, or perhaps earlier, we shall, given a continuation of the present policy, be facing a fuel bill with the Arab countries and Venezuela of $6.5 billion at today's prices. We shall have to generate this amount by means which are not obvious at this point in time because we are already running tremendous trade deficits in the manufacturing sector.
Since this $6.5 billion is being used to pay for consumer imports, the expenditure represents a direct loss to the Canadian economy, one which can be translated into lost jobs and so on. What will happen to the value of our dollar when the nation is subjected to a continued drain of that nature? It might well drop to 85 cents or to 80 cents. What will be the effect on the cost of living of the increased price of the goods we are obliged to import?
Canada has the geological potential to be self-sufficient, to be independent of the political intricacies of the Middle East oil trade. Since we are not obliged to pay out these large sums of money, every opportunity for self-sufficiency should be seized and pursued. The minister has suggested we would be opposed to importing cheap oil from secure sources. That is an absurd statement. But would the hon. gentleman like to tell us where we can find cheap oil from secure sources today?

speechtext: That is self-reliance.

speechtext:
That is producing as much as we consume and it means a change in priorities. In my opinion the attitude of the government has not changed since 1973, when the first energy policy was produced. It still holds the view that the prime function of the oil and gas producers is to be a source of revenue for the federal treasury. An examination of policy statements, an examination of the motivation behind this bill, leave one with the impression that the role of government is
Business of the House
considered to be that of taking as much of the pie as possible. Of course, to change the metaphor, they do not want to kill the goose altogether, but their attitude remains unchanged: it is to take as much of the pie as possible. A government which views the issue in this way is guilty of distorted perception, because the first priority is to achieve self-sufficiency-to produce as much as we consume. We are, of course, dealing here with the total package, not just with oil and gas.
This is not the type of bill we welcome with great enthusiasm but it is not one which invites very much opposition either, so we shall not hinder its passage. Nevertheless, there are aspects which cause concern. To begin with, I question the motives for bringing it forward in the first place since the information which the government now seeks to compel companies to provide is already being given voluntarily. This has been the case for five or six years. Why bring out the whip when, all this time, the carrot has proven to be effective? Why these compulsory tactics?
Then again, the clause which would permit the minister to disclose confidential information when he deemed it to be in the public interest is abhorrent on philosophical grounds. Is the next step to be the disclosure by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay) of confidential information supplied by taxpayers on the ground that it would be in the public interest to do so? Corporations are not anonymous bodies despite the inclination to regard them as such. There are people involved-employers, workers, shareholders. If the minister were to use the blackmailing capability provided by the clause to which I have referred, it might be a comfort to him to think he was using it only against corporations, but he would be using it against people, the people who own and manage and work for these companies. As I say, the clause is abhorrent.
Another clause which I find abhorrent is that which would allow officials to burst in and seize records should the minister believe there was reason to do so. We know what happens when officials are armed with powers of this sort; I hardly need to explain why provisions of this kind should be opposed.
In our opinion, this bill is another candidate for a "sunset clause". We see no reason why this legislation should still be on the books 50, 60 or 100 years from now after we have used up all our petroleum and are relying on solar power or nuclear fission. We do not like the idea of some official sitting in a back room compiling forms and having them filled out simply because that is what the law says. Let us limit the life of the bill to five or six years; if the government thinks its operation should be extended it could be done at that time. I have no doubt parliament would agree to consider whether it should be extended or not.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that it is four o'clock.

subsubtopic: STUDY AND IDENTIFICATION OF NEEDS OF SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
that Bill C-218, respecting senior citizens, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, senior citizens of Canada, working in far more difficult times than we have experienced, have created for us a better way of life than they themselves enjoyed. For many senior citizens living in their golden years the sands of time are running swiftly. The opportunity for us to recognize their contribution to our society is limited in time, and every day we wait this opportunity decreases dramatically. That is why I have introduced this bill.
I suggest that there is a need for a commission as a full-time job to identify the needs of senior citizens. These needs are very visible and large in number. I would like to mention a few of them.
The first problem that comes to mind is that of poverty. Many senior citizens grew up in the hungry thirties when pension plans were few and old age security was difficult to buy. Pension plans that were available did not envisage today's high prices and dramatic increases in the cost of living. Large numbers of our senior citizens are living below the poverty line, and the sole source of income for many of them is the old age pension and supplement. Their meagre incomes are ravaged by inflation. The cost of living, particularly food, clothing, shelter, energy and heat costs, have risen very rapidly, causing economic hardship and mental anguish. These costs increase faster than the increase in the old age pension and supplement. For workers who are being retired earlier than age 65 the present old age pension system offers no assistance, and these early retired workers suffer an unfair hardship.
How do we define poverty? There are four poverty lines defined by three independent organizations. They each provide unofficial measures which are useful in assessing poverty by income level. The Economic Council of Canada in its fifth report used the Statistics Canada approach to measuring poverty: a family is poor if it spends 70 per cent or more of its income on food, clothing and shelter. The Special Senate Committee on Poverty judged that this criterion was not satisfactory as a permanent yardstick of poverty.
In 1973 Statistics Canada revised its poverty line. It decided that family is poor if it spends 62 per cent or more of its income on basic essentials.
The Senate committee formula and that used by the Canadian Council on Social Development put poverty levels at 50 per cent of average Canadian family income with varying adjustments for inflation, taxes and gross national product.
There is no official poverty line; at best, any measure will be faulty. Last March Senator David Croll, Chairman of the Special Senate Committee on Poverty, put on record the 1976 poverty line using the four bases.
January 27, 1978

In the year 2031 there will be 8 million elderly Canadians. Those people are alive now. Some 2 million Canadians today are old age pensioners. In eight years' time that figure will rise to 3 million. Some two thirds of them, according to a recent Global Television feature program, are living below the poverty line. In its July, 1976 paper on the changing age structure the Science Council notes at page 3 the following:
The most glaring fact in regard to the distribution of income by age, and one which promises to be perpetuated in the future, is the relative poverty of the aged, compared with other age cohorts-
In 1974, 26 per cent of old age pensioners received the full GIS and 32 per cent received a partial supplement. Thus over one half of Canada's elderly needed supplementary income to bring them at least to the poverty line.
It is true that the apparent poverty of the aged is somewhat mitigated by the fact that many of the elderly own outright such assets as a home or car. However, these tend to be of older vintage and thus have a greater likelihood of incurring maintenance costs. In inflationary times, the burden of escalating repair costs and taxes can be nearly intolerable to a person on a small fixed income (i.e., pension).
The aged are our poorest population group, women being the worst off. Kevin Collins, senior economist for the Canadian Congress of Labour, says of his recent study for the Canadian Council on Social Development that, and I quote:
If you look at all the different population groups, like young people, single parents, the elderly, it's the elderly who are the poorest. But among the elderly, it's the women who are the poorest of the poorest.
Mr. Collins said that in an interview published in the Globe and Mail on January 13, 1978 at page 12. Mr. Collins was the program director of income securities at the council. His year-long study on women and pensions was his last council project. Rather than recommending pension reforms that relate exclusively to women, the study calls for changes in the private and public pension plan systems and slams the federal government for its old age security and guaranteed income supplement benefits program. Mr. Collins said of this program:
It guarantees a level of income for the elderly that is inadequate. It's below any realistic poverty line. In other words, it guarantees poverty.
One of the study's many recommendations calls for the combined income guarantee for the elderly to be substantially increased to meet 1977 poverty lines, which the Canadian Council on Social Development has estimated at $4,400 a year for a single person, and $7,300 for a couple.
Statistics Canada's booklet "Income Distribution by Size in Canada", published in October, 1977, reports that in 1976 31 per cent of single persons over 65 and of families headed by persons of that age, taken together, earned less than $4,000; half of them received less than $3,000 yearly. About 62 per cent of individuals aged 65 or more earned less than $4,000; 42 per cent earned less than $3,000.
If we agree that this is a legitimate problem of senior citizens, what do we do about it? I personally feel for one thing that the old age security pension should be increased to $200 per month immediately and that the guaranteed income supplement should be increased proportionately. I feel too that old age security should be made available to persons 60 years of
Senior Citizens
age and over who are retired and that the supplement be paid to those who otherwise qualify at that age.
The cost of living index should be amended to fully reflect the increase in the cost of living to senior citizens. The basic requirements of senior citizens pretty well gobble up their slender incomes and it is these basic requirements, food, heat, light, shelter and clothing, that should be used as the criterion for indexing the old age pension and supplement. I am suggesting that the increase in these staple items should be averaged and form the multiplier for indexing the old age pension and supplement.
I feel too that the spouse's allowance should be continued for any spouse aged 60 and over who is widowed. The spouse of a public service pensioner gets one-half of the pension when the pensioner dies, but the fixed costs of living, including real property, tax, heat, light, repairs, telephone, all continue unabated. This is a cruel and merciless provision that should be rectified.
It is a blot on the conscience of this nation that our disabled war veterans did not receive the full increase in their pensions related to parity with the control group of five categories of public servants, instead of the increase being related to the much lower consumer price index. I sincerely hope this tragic error in judgment will be rectified.
The world of the senior citizen is sometimes much smaller and shrinks much faster in terms of friends and acquaintances that it does with younger people who are more active and make their way in the world.
Barbara Reynolds, in a paper entitled "Problems of Aging", produced by our own research library, May 3, 1974, reports that only about 5 per cent of those aged 65 or more need to live in institutions and that most elderly persons are reasonably healthy. Hence feebleness, sickness and other mental or physical handicaps are not the dominant obstacle to the good life for most elderly poor folk. Their critical need is for a chance to better themselves.
The Special Senate Committee on Poverty commented that Canada has spent billions on income security and welfare programs to little purpose. They have "only made the lives of the poor a little less desperate". The committee's report continues:
While the poor lack many things, their most fundamental lack is one of opportunity-of the liberty to exercise meaningful choice in our economy and our society. If they had that liberty, in ampler measure than today, they, or at any rate their children, would perform the greater part of the job of lifting themselves out of poverty.
In short, we cannot expect major accomplishments unless we guarantee the necessary preconditions of sufficiency and opportunity.
In each generation there are some poor people who are able to escape from poverty against all the odds and obstacles. But for most, it is simply impossible to control their economic destinies.
It will continue to be impossible unless we find the means to increase their choice, to expand their liberty . .. and to convince them that they were not born to the "small loaf'.
It seems to me, with high vacancy rates in our air carrier and land transportation systems, that senior citizens should be encouraged to do some travelling to visit friends, relatives and

January 27, 1978
Senior Citizens
see our great country, and that when they travel in Canada they should enjoy a 50 per cent reduction in fares.
Another basic need of senior citizens is accommodation, but there surely can be no substitute for senior citizens remaining in their own homes as long as they wish and are physically able to do so. Competent but poor old folk often end up in nursing homes because they cannot pay for low-care or no-care housing. In 1976 in Ontario, according to provincial health minister Frank Miller, there were 35,000 persons in homes for the aged who should not have been there.
In earlier times they might well have been with younger members of their family, looking after grandchildren with a room of their own in the bigger homes of those days. But today the families are smaller, houses have shrunk and costs have climbed. The system tends to discard older persons.
Even elderly people living in their own houses are forced to sell because they cannot keep up the property taxes. They get a good price in inflated dollars for the family house but, in Ottawa, many have to pay more than $600 monthly for board and a shared room in an old folks' home subsidized by the province. It is a "no-win" situation especially for a childless person who has paid school taxes for decades and now is forced out by taxes.
It may be hard for older persons to keep a house; even harder to buy one if they need financing. Banks and trust companies generally do not issue mortgages on properties if the sum of the applicant's age and the term of the loan exceeds 80.
City planners and developers appear to favour destroying whatever has lost the glitter of newness. They raze the old to make way for sterile, costly apartments renting at prices beyond the reach of the elderly. Governments too seem mesmerized by the passion to plant huge office buildings in city cores, whether or not there is a valid demand for offices. Kicking out the poor and old on the pretext of upgrading an area is more fashionable than renewing accommodation so that the elderly may stay in districts they know and love among friends of a lifetime.
I suggest strongly one need that can be identified is the need to meet expenses and be financially able to continue living in one's own home on a slender retirement allowance. Personally I think this type of living should be encouraged and, if necessary, financial assistance should be given to senior citizens to enable them to do this. One goal of our nation should be to see that our senior citizens receive at least the average of the minimum wages established across the country.
For disabled senior citizens who require nursing home care, existing facilities are not sufficient to meet the demand. The financial technique presently used to build these facilities is to borrow money from CMHC, obtain federal grants where they are available and construct the facility. About 80 per cent of the cost of operating these facilities in New Brunswick is paid for by the provincial government through social assistance programs. In making these operating payments the provincial

government in effect repays the CMHC mortgage to a great extent.
The federal government has not come to grips with this problem to the financial degree it should, and I would think the great need for facilities like this would attract the early attention of the commission that I propose be set up by this bill. I can indicate that in my own riding, areas such as Stanley, Millville, Nackawic, Oromocto and Fredericton come quickly to mind. There are many others as well. I would like to see greater use made along these lines of the Victoria Health Centre in Fredericton. Wherever possible senior citizens should be located in or near their own communities.
One project that appeared in the Canada Works program in my constituency and which I should like to share with the House is one involving a one-on-one service by volunteers for senior citizens. The volunteer under this program would be available to assist a senior citizen, who perhaps is unable to get out of his or her home, with such things as grocery shopping or shovelling out a front walk on a bad winter day. This type of service I find extremely useful and is appreciated by senior citizens.
Mr. A. Allentuck in "The Cost of Age", Toronto, Fitzhenry & Whitside, 1977, prescribes single-issue politics as a powerful weapon in the hands of the elderly of the future. "More for the elderly now" might be their motif. Their platform contains the following elements:
1.	No compulsory retirement.
2.	Private pensions openly managed and properly insured against mismanagement and fraud.
3.	Public pensions, principally the Guaranteed Income Supplement, increased to levels adequate to support lives that are comfortable and secure.
4.	Relief from real estate taxes.
5.	Construction of more and better nursing homes.
6.	Reduction of the cost of eyeglasses, hearing aids and other prosthetic devices either by subsidy or government intervention into the respective industries.
In the same book Mr. Allentuck suggests the following:
1.	Patients shall be treated, dressed, clothed, housed and cared for in a manner befitting their stature as adults.
2.	Patients may refuse medical treatments and medication to the extent permitted by law.
3.	Patients shall not be compelled to participate in any experiments of any nature.
4.	Patients shall be given explanations of their conditions, care and treatment, and such explanations shall be phrased in terms comprehensible to them.
5.	Patients shall not be restricted to their beds or to their institutions unless their medical conditions so warrant.
6.	If patients or their families make supplemental contributions to their institutions as entrance contract payments, such payments shall be refunded if they withdraw in protest against service rendered.
7.	The patient's religious and cultural preferences shall be respected.
Mr. Reuben Baetz, when executive director of the Canadian Council on Social Development, had the following to say about the elderly:
Retired persons must themselves be engaged in the planning and implementation of programs, services, recreation, education, from which they are to derive
January 27, 1978

benefit. Why can't the aged be more involved in the operation of homes for the aged? The revolution against paternalism is now well advanced on the university campus. The students are no longer ready to have handed down to them an education which the university fathers feel is best for them. They insist on being involved .... It is therefore high time that the aged assert clearly and forthrightly that they too want to be masters of their own destiny. They should make it perfectly clear that they too have human rights which must be protected and enhanced, and that these rights are more than a pension sufficient to keep body and soul together. They include the right to dignity and self-respect. In many cases, to protect these rights, they must have the opportunity to continue to make meaningful contributions to society. The decision as to when, how, and how long an individual should continue to participate in the mainstream of society must be made by that individual, and not by some computer clock which "rings down the curtain" at age 65.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of this bill because I am so well aware of how terribly difficult it is for most senior citizens to live on what is provided for them now. It is difficult especially for them at a time when there is an increase in the cost of living on a year to year basis of 9.5 per cent. They despair when they see the cost of living increase to some 11.5 per cent, which is what happened during the last three months.
The basic amount of old age security is presently up to a little over $150 per month, and there is a $105 per month guaranteed income supplement for those who have nothing to live on. Therefore, $150 a month is paid to everyone 65 years of age or over, and $255 is paid to those who have the supplement. During these times of very high cost of living, the least one could hope for is an increase in the basic amount of old age security from $200 a month during this year, with a goal of $250 or $300 by 1980.
The guaranteed income supplement should be raised also this year to at least $130 a month, with a goal of $175 by 1982. This would be no great fiscal or financial burden on the nation, since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has indicated that the growth in real terms this year will be 5 per cent. These figures would be the minimum amount of rough justice the younger citizens of Canada owe to older people who are no longer in the labour force. Just as young union employees are often hesitant to vote for increases in the pension plan under the collective bargaining process and prefer immediate wages, we find creeping into our social thinking the notion that the nation is doing about as well as it can for those citizens who built this country during extremely trying times and suffered greatly during the depression and wars.
There are a great number of senior citizens, some of whom are veterans of World War I and others veterans of World War II. On June 28, 1973 royal assent was given to Bill C-202, which provided for an increase in the basic war disability pension to an amount equivalent to the composite of five public service categories. At that time it was felt that the Department of Veterans Affairs finally had arrived at an equitable basic rate of pension. A recent announcement by that department indicated an increase of 7.2 per cent. That fails to fulfil the spirit of the legislation passed in June of 1973, because the government did not repeal section 58.1 and 58.2 of the Pension Act. Bill C-202 increased the basic rate for veterans in an amount which was equal to the average wages of the composite group I have referred to. However, the
Senior Citizens
provision remained in the Pension Act for increases in the years following the approval of Bill C-202 to be based only on the Consumer Price Index.
In comparing the basic rate of pension of a war disability pensioner, who is totally disabled, with the average wages for the composite group of five in the Public Service of Canada, there is a differential of approximately $600 to $700 on a yearly basis in favour of public servants. The government should take steps this year to close this differential, if it has any sense of gratitude for the veterans. Whether the government uses this during a political campaign or not is of little importance; the fairness and the spirit of the June 1973 legislation should be adhered to by the government.
A few weeks ago I was surprised to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) say, in reply to a question before the House, that the spouse's allowance providing for a payment to either a man or woman between the ages of 60 and 65 would apply only to a spouse who is married to, or living with, an older pensioner and would not be changed to include single people, whether widowed or unmarried. This is completely ridiculous when one considers that the total cost of including these categories would be approximately $4 million a year.
Recently in my constituency office a spinster, who was 62 years of age, said: "If I lived in a common law marriage with someone, I could get this allowance". People feel incensed about this kind of discrimination with regard to the present spouse's allowances. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in answering the question, said that one of the reasons for her refusal to include these people would be national pressure to reduce to 60 the age at which old age security benefits are granted, and she said that the government could not afford that. This is a lame excuse for not including the above categories of people who are now being discriminated against.
Like Sweden, Canada should have a national study which would embrace the notion that people should be allowed to retire at various pension levels between the ages of 60 and 70, if not 75. Many senior citizens in Canada, including women who are heads of households, are suffering badly under our national and provincial assistance system. The low income groups in this country, such as, for example, the bottom 20 per cent of our income earners, receive only 4.4 per cent of our national pie, called the GNP, while the top 20 per cent skim some 40 per cent off that pie. That should concern us as parliamentarians and we should determine to really do something about it. I do not care if it is done in an election year or at another time. There is a great need for us as Canadians to provide a sufficient income for senior citizens who have done so much for this nation. Let us as parliamentarians accept the responsibility for bringing in needed reforms, not next year or the following year, but now, in 1978.

subsubtopic: STUDY AND IDENTIFICATION OF NEEDS OF SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have

January 27, 1978
Senior Citizens
the opportunity to speak on Bill C-218 which was introduced by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). Like him, I too have great concern about the needs of the senior citizens, but in reading Bill C-218, one wonders what the proposed senior citizens' commission could be expected to accomplish. The bill states that the commission is to study and identify the needs of senior citizens and make recommendations concerning these needs to the governor in council.
The establishment of a commission such as that proposed in the bill would more appropriately be a matter for action by the provinces. Indeed, some provincial governments have appointed bodies to identify the needs of older people, make recommendations on how these needs can be met, serve in an advisory capacity in the establishment of programs and services to meet the needs, identify gaps in information and services, promote research, and, in some cases, carry out research. Called by any one of several names, such as senior citizens commission, advisory council, or provincial senior citizens council, these bodies are appointed by government and responsible to a provincial minister of the Crown.
Several provinces have bodies operating under voluntary auspices either as independent councils on aging or as divisions of provincial social planning councils. In some urban centres, similar structures have been organized locally. In addition, some provinces have an office, bureau or division on aging, usually located in the department of social services. All these bodies are engaged in identifying the needs of older people and in establishing, in co-operation with other bodies, services for them.
Such developments are not surprising when the needs of older people are considered, namely, economic needs, physical and mental health, nutrition, living arrangements, transportation, leisure activities, education, employment, retirement and spiritual wellbeing. The federal government's responsibility in the economic sphere is fully recognized. Furthermore, federal financial participation with the provinces in the development of health and social services as well as the construction of housing and institutional care facilities has been in effect for many years. But the fact is that health and social services, housing, institutional care facilities, education and so on, are all under provincial jurisdiction.
There are those who argue that if older people were provided with enough money, they could look after their own needs. We have heard some of that rhetoric this afternoon. This is a fallacious argument. It assumes that the services needed are available, that they are accessible, and that whatever their cost old people could afford to pay for them regardless of the quantity required or the length of time the services are needed. The recognition of the lack of supportive services to help elderly persons to live independently in their own community, despite socioeconomic and physical problems, was the motive behind the federal government's initiative in introducing the social services act in Bill C-57 during the second session of the thirtieth parliament.
